mt_gorilla_block.blurb: A small cluster of boulders tucked into a wooded pocket over a low hill, part of the Sagebrush Point bouldering zone beside Highway 191 in Gallatin Canyon south of Bozeman. Ten problems are described, running from V0 up to V4 with the bulk around V2, so it suits climbers who want a quick session rather than a full day. The front face is known for hard, technical moves, while the back side offers a pleasant arete. Several lines have sit-start variations, including a compression start and a dyno. Bring pads and expect a short, easy walk in.

mt_shredder_wall.blurb: A sport wall in Rattler Gulch, a limestone canyon east of Missoula reached from the Bearmouth exit of I-90 and a dirt road. Nine of the ten routes are bolted sport lines and one is trad. Grades start at 5.10 and climb through the 5.11s and 5.12s to a single 5.13, with a handful of well-liked moderates that make it a good second stop after the nearby Sidewinder section. The wall is vertical to slightly less than vertical, with pockets, jugs and crimps. The canyon is tight, so it can run cold in the off-season and warm in midsummer.

mt_tiger_stripe.blurb: In the Bitterroot Valley at Mill Creek, this steep North Rim wall sits uphill, between the Tick Farm and Big Science. It holds about ten routes, almost all bolted sport lines of one pitch, from a 5.7 up through a cluster of 5.10s, 5.11s and a few 5.12s, plus one aid line. The climbing is powerful and pumpy, on golden, high-quality rock with long reaches and bouldery cruxes. Black streaks can stay wet after storms. Some lines share anchors, so check which route you are on before lowering.

mt_under_the_sea_wall.blurb: The tallest and busiest wall in Lower Bear Canyon, in the hills outside Bozeman. All ten routes are bolted sport lines, with about a route for every grade from 5.8 to 5.10, so it works well for building confidence on moderates. The wall catches sun for most of the day with some shade early and late, which makes it pleasant in cool weather and warm in summer. Reaching it means crossing the creek on a log and taking the left fork toward the tall formation. Expect company on evenings and weekends.

mt_south_stone_wall.blurb: A south-facing sport wall in the Stone Hill climbing area of northwest Montana, above Highway 37. It is almost entirely bolted, and the ten routes are mostly moderate: a few easy 5.7s and 5.8s, then a run of 5.9s and 5.10s, with one 5.12 for the stronger climber. That mix makes it friendly for newer leaders. The trail starts at the road and the wall is under a ten minute walk, so it is easy to fit in a short outing. Being south-facing, it gets plenty of sun.

mt_uphill_areas.blurb: One of four sectors at The Palace, Red Lodge's biggest concentration of limestone sport climbing, perched above Palisade Campground. This sector holds around ten bolted routes, mostly 5.10, with one 5.9 and a few 5.11s and a single 5.12. The rock is fair and still being developed, and the climbing ranges from short, fun lines to longer, more continuous ones that reward careful footwork and reading small features. The trail up is steep, with switchbacks and some side-hilling, and this sector lies about ten minutes beyond the main area. A stick clip can be useful.
